facts.text: Premiere: Rome, 14 January 1900. Postponed a day for fear of unrest. Rome being Rome.
evidence: It premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome on 14 January 1900.
its first performance was delayed for a day for fear of disturbances
facts.plain: Tosca premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome on 14 January 1900, a day late, because of fears of unrest.

facts.text: Opening night came with an anarchist bomb warning. The conductor’s emergency plan: play the royal march.
facts.evidence: Police received warnings of an anarchist bombing of the theatre, and instructed Mugnone
facts.plain: Police had warnings of an anarchist bomb at the premiere. The conductor, Mugnone, was told to strike up the royal march in an emergency.

facts.text: Critics: lukewarm. Audiences: twenty straight performances to packed houses. Guess who won.
evidence: Much of the critical and press reaction was lukewarm
the premiere was followed by twenty performances, all given to packed houses
facts.plain: The critics were lukewarm, but the public loved it: the premiere was followed by twenty performances, all to packed houses.

facts.text: Puccini, 1889, on why Tosca: “no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle.” Stay for the Te Deum.
facts.attribution: Puccini, letter to Giulio Ricordi, 7 May 1889 (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: I see in this Tosca the opera I need, with no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle
facts.plain: Puccini begged his publisher in 1889 to get Sardou’s permission: “I see in this Tosca the opera I need, with no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle.”

facts.text: Young Enrico Caruso hoped to create Cavaradossi. They picked someone “more experienced”.
facts.evidence: The young Enrico Caruso had hoped to create the role of Cavaradossi, but was passed over in favour of the more experienced Emilio De Marchi.
facts.plain: The young Enrico Caruso hoped to create Cavaradossi but was passed over for the more experienced Emilio De Marchi.

facts.text: No overture. Three chords (Scarpia’s theme) and a fugitive bursts in. Puccini skips the small talk.
facts.evidence: The opera begins without any prelude; the opening chords of the Scarpia motif lead immediately to the agitated appearance of Angelotti
facts.plain: There is no prelude: the opening chords are Scarpia’s motif, and Angelotti bursts straight in.

facts.text: Mid-Te Deum, in church, Scarpia sings: “Tosca, you make me forget even God!” Read the room.
facts.evidence: Tosca, you make me forget even God!
facts.plain: As the Te Deum procession fills the church, Scarpia joins the prayer: “Tosca, you make me forget even God!”

facts.text: Maria Jeritza fell escaping Scarpia and sang “Vissi d’arte” from the floor. It worked, so she kept doing it.
evidence: was said to be Puccini's favorite Tosca
Jeritza was the first to deliver "Vissi d'arte" from a prone position, having fallen to the stage while eluding the grasp of Scarpia.
Jeritza sang the aria while on the floor thereafter
facts.plain: Maria Jeritza, said to be Puccini’s favorite Tosca, once fell while escaping Scarpia and sang “Vissi d’arte” lying on the floor. It was such a success that she kept doing it.

facts.text: Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear the real matins bells, then had bells cast by four foundries.
evidence: went to the Castel Sant'Angelo to measure the sound of matins bells there
Puccini had bells for the Roman dawn cast to order by four different foundries.
facts.plain: For the Roman dawn, Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear the matins bells, and had bells cast by four different foundries.

facts.text: Librettist Illica, after the premiere: all that fuss and money on the bells “passes completely unnoticed”. Listen anyway.
facts.attribution: Luigi Illica, letter to Ricordi (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: the great fuss and the large amount of money for the bells have constituted an additional folly, because it passes completely unnoticed
facts.plain: Librettist Illica grumbled after the premiere that all the fuss and money spent on the bells “passes completely unnoticed”.

facts.text: The shepherd boy sings in Roman dialect. Puccini asked for a “good romanesco poet” and got folklorist Giggi Zanazzo.
evidence: The composer asked a friend to have a "good romanesco poet" write some words
Luigi "Giggi" Zanazzo wrote the verse
facts.plain: The shepherd boy’s song is in Roman dialect. Puccini asked for a “good romanesco poet”, and folklorist Giggi Zanazzo wrote the verse.

facts.text: Part of this duet is recycled from music Puccini cut from his opera Edgar. His publisher noticed. Too late.
evidence: some of the music for Cavaradossi's act 3 aria, "O dolci mani" was borrowed from music Puccini had cut from his early opera, Edgar
time was too short before the scheduled January 1900 premiere to make any further changes
facts.plain: Ricordi noticed that part of “O dolci mani” was borrowed from music Puccini had cut from his early opera Edgar, and demanded changes. There wasn’t time.

facts.text: Joseph Kerman: a “shabby little shocker”. Thomas Beecham: anything Kerman says about Puccini “can safely be ignored”.
evidence: described Tosca as a "shabby little shocker."
can safely be ignored
facts.plain: In the 1950s musicologist Joseph Kerman called Tosca a “shabby little shocker”. Conductor Thomas Beecham replied that anything Kerman says about Puccini “can safely be ignored”.

facts.text: Met premiere: 4 February 1901, barely a year after Rome. New York didn’t wait.
facts.evidence: The premiere at the Metropolitan Opera was on 4 February 1901
facts.plain: The Met premiere was on 4 February 1901, only a year after the world premiere.

facts.text: Pavarotti’s final stage performance: Cavaradossi, at the Met, 13 March 2004.
facts.evidence: Pavarotti's last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.
facts.plain: Luciano Pavarotti’s last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.

facts.text: Sardou wrote La Tosca for Sarah Bernhardt. Over 3,000 performances in France alone. Big shoes.
facts.evidence: with more than 3,000 performances in France alone
facts.plain: Sardou’s play La Tosca, written for Sarah Bernhardt, had more than 3,000 performances in France alone.

facts.text: A biographer’s summary: “three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama.” Enjoy!
facts.attribution: Mary Jane Phillips-Matz, Puccini biography (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: leaving three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama
facts.plain: By cutting several numbers, Puccini left “three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama”, as his biographer put it.

facts.text: Queen Margherita attended the premiere. She arrived after Act I.
evidence: as did Queen Margherita, though she arrived late, after the first act

facts.text: Premiere night, moments in: latecomers caused a commotion, someone yelled “Bring down the curtain!”, and the orchestra stopped.
evidence: caused by latecomers attempting to enter the auditorium, and a shout of "Bring down the curtain!", at which Mugnone stopped the orchestra

facts.text: Why trust the conductor with the bomb plan? Mugnone had already survived a theatre bombing in Barcelona.
evidence: (who had survived a theatre bombing in Barcelona)

facts.text: Tosca was first assigned to Alberto Franchetti. One story: Ricordi talked him out of it as too violent to stage.
evidence: which Ricordi then assigned to the composer Alberto Franchetti
One story relates that Ricordi convinced Franchetti that the work was too violent to be successfully staged.

facts.text: Angelotti’s escape plan: disguise himself as a woman, in clothes his sister left in the chapel.
evidence: his plan to flee disguised as a woman, using clothes left in the chapel by his sister

facts.sceneMatch: ^Act II$|Tosca è un buon falco|Ha più forte
facts.text: That distant gavotte? Puccini adapted a student exercise by his late brother Michele, so he could “live again”.
evidence: For this music Puccini adapted a fifteen-year-old student exercise by his late brother, Michele, stating that in this way his brother could live again through him.

facts.text: The first Tosca, Hariclea Darclée, came billed as “accomplished (but temperamental)”. Typecasting.
evidence: The accomplished (but temperamental) soprano Hariclea Darclée was selected for the title role

facts.text: Puccini said fans of this aria owe him thrice, partly for refusing advice to throw it “in the waste-paper basket”.
evidence: for declining expert advice to throw the result in the waste-paper basket

facts.text: Tosca coaches Mario on how to play dead, because the firing squad will use blanks. What could go wrong?
evidence: Tosca then anxiously coaches Cavaradossi on how to play dead when the firing squad shoots at him with blanks.

facts.text: An 1896 draft ended with Tosca going mad, imagining she and Mario are on a gondola. Sardou said no.
evidence: The 1896 libretto also offers a different ending, in which Tosca does not die but instead goes mad.
she and her Mario are on a gondola
Sardou refused to consider this change

facts.text: Kerman on the final bars: “Tosca leaps, and the orchestra screams the first thing that comes into its head.”
evidence: Tosca leaps, and the orchestra screams the first thing that comes into its head.

facts.text: Opera legend: a crew swapped Tosca’s landing mattress for a trampoline. She reportedly came up 15 times.
facts.attribution: Los Angeles Times, 9 Jan 1990 (citing Hugh Vickers, “Great Opera Disasters”)
evidence: But the crew had replaced the mattress with a trampoline.
she came up 15 times before the curtain fell

facts.text: Maria Callas first sang Tosca at 18, in Greek, in Athens, 1942.
evidence: Callas had first sung Tosca at age 18 in a performance given in Greek, in the Greek National Opera in Athens on 27 August 1942.

facts.text: Zeffirelli’s 1964 Covent Garden Tosca (Callas and Gobbi) stayed in use for more than 40 years. Durable sets.
evidence: her performances at the Royal Opera House in 1964, with Tito Gobbi as Scarpia
This production, by Franco Zeffirelli, remained in continuous use at Covent Garden for more than 40 years

facts.text: Paris, 1903: Gabriel Fauré was offended by Tosca’s “disconcerting vulgarities”. You’ve been warned.
evidence: Gabriel Fauré was offended by "disconcerting vulgarities"
